- **Romans 8:34** – *“Christ Jesus is the one who died—more than that, who was raised—who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us.”*

### 6. Warnings That Presuppose Perseverance
Scripture also contains warnings about falling away, which serve as a means by which God preserves His people. The reality of true perseverance is shown in passages that distinguish genuine faith from temporary profession.

- **1 John 2:19** – *“They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.”* (Those who permanently depart never truly belonged.)
- **Hebrews 3:14** – *“For we have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end.”* (Perseverance is the evidence of genuine participation in Christ.)

### Summary
The doctrine does not teach that Christians never sin or struggle, but that God infallibly preserves true believers so that they will persevere in faith and repentance until the end. It is grounded in the Father’s purpose, the Son’s redemption and intercession, and the Spirit’s sealing and indwelling.

questions.question: What verses support the doctrine of total depravity?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 3:10-12, Eph 2:1-3, Gen 6:5
questions.response:
The doctrine of total depravity (also called total inability) does not mean that humans are as evil as they could possibly be, but that sin affects the whole person—mind, will, and emotions—rendering them unable to save themselves or to choose God apart from His grace. Here are the key verses commonly cited in support of this doctrine:

**1. The universal condition of the heart**
- **Jeremiah 17:9** – “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?”

**2. Spiritual death and bondage to sin**
- **Ephesians 2:1–3** – “And you were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked… and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind.”  
- **Colossians 2:13** – “And you, who were dead in your trespasses… God made alive together with him.”

**3. Inability to seek God or do good (in a saving sense)**
- **Romans 3:10–12** – “None is righteous, no, not one; no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one.”
- **John 6:44** – “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.”

**4. The mind set on the flesh is hostile to God**
- **Romans 8:7–8** – “For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.”

**5. Inability to understand spiritual things**
- **1 Corinthians 2:14** – “The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.”

**6. Evil actions come from within**
- **Mark 7:21–23** – “For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder… All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person.”

**7. The universality of sin and its consequences**
- **Psalm 51:5** – “Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me.”  
- **Romans 5:12** – “Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned.”
- **Genesis 6:5** – “The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.”

These verses together paint a picture of humanity as spiritually dead, enslaved to sin, and unable to turn to God apart from His initiating and regenerating grace.

questions.question: Which passages teach justification by faith alone?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 3:28, Eph 2:8-9, Gal 2:16
questions.response:
Here are the key New Testament passages most commonly cited regarding justification by faith, along with brief explanatory notes.

### Primary Passages on Justification by Faith

These passages explicitly link justification with faith, often contrasting it with works of the law.

- **Romans 3:28** – “For we maintain that a person is justified by faith apart from the works of the law.”
    This is the most direct statement that justification occurs through faith, not by observing the Mosaic law.

- **Romans 5:1** – “Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
    Faith is the instrumental means by which we receive justification and its resulting peace.

- **Galatians 2:16** – “Know that a person is not justified by the works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ. So we, too, have put our faith in Christ Jesus that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the law, because by the works of the law no one will be justified.”
    This verse three times emphasizes that justification is by faith in Christ and not by legal observance.

- **Galatians 3:11** – “Clearly no one who relies on the law is justified before God, because ‘the righteous will live by faith.’”
    Quoting Habakkuk 2:4, Paul argues that the principle of justification by faith was always God’s plan.

- **Philippians 3:9** – “And be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ—the righteousness that comes from God on the basis of faith.”
    Paul contrasts self-derived righteousness with the righteousness God gives through faith.

### The Example of Abraham

Paul argues that Abraham’s experience establishes the pattern for all believers.

- **Romans 4:2-5** – “If, in fact, Abraham was justified by works, he had something to boast about—but not before God. What does Scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.’ Now to the one who works, wages are not credited as a gift but as an obligation. However, to the one who does not work but trusts God who justifies the ungodly, their faith is credited as righteousness.”
    This passage explicitly separates faith from works in the act of justification, defining it as a gift received by trust.

- **Galatians 3:6-9** – “So also Abraham ‘believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.’ Understand, then, that those who have faith are children of Abraham. Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and announced the gospel in advance to Abraham: ‘All nations will be blessed through you.’ So those who rely on faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.”
    Abraham’s justification by faith is the model for both Jews and Gentiles.

### Salvation by Grace Through Faith

These passages emphasize that the entire salvation process, including justification, is a gift received through faith, totally apart from human effort.

- **Ephesians 2:8-9** – “For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith—and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God—not by works, so that no one can boast.”
    While not using the word “justified,” this text clarifies that the entire salvation package, including justification, is a gift of God received through faith.

- **Titus 3:5-7** – “He saved us, not because of righteous things we had done, but because of his mercy. He saved us through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us generously through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs having the hope of eternal life.”
    God’s mercy, not human deeds, is the cause; faith is the means by which we receive this justification.

### The Explicit Statement of “Faith Alone”

While “faith alone” (*sola fide*) is implied throughout, James’s epistle is the only place the exact phrase occurs.

- **James 2:24** – “You see that a person is considered righteous by what they do and not by faith alone.”
    **Important Note**: This is the only verse in Scripture using the exact phrase “faith alone,” and it appears to deny it. The historic Protestant interpretation (from Luther onward) is that Paul speaks of justification *before God* by a living faith that trusts Christ, while James speaks of the vindication or evidence of that faith *before people* by works. Thus, Paul uses “justify” in a declarative, once-for-all sense, while James uses “justify” in a demonstrative or evidential sense (as seen in Abraham’s later act of offering Isaac, which “fulfilled” the faith that justified him 30 years earlier in Genesis 15:6). This distinction is key to understanding the harmony between Paul and James.

### Old Testament Foundation

The New Testament teaching is rooted in the Old Testament.

- **Habakkuk 2:4** – “See, the enemy is puffed up; his desires are not upright—but the righteous person will live by his faithfulness.”
    This verse is the cornerstone of Paul’s argument in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11. It established the principle that faith, not ethnic identity or law-keeping, is the mark of the righteous.

- **Genesis 15:6** – “Abram believed the LORD, and he credited it to him as righteousness.”
    This is the foundational event of justification by faith, quoted multiple times in the New Testament (Romans 4:3, 22; Galatians 3:6). This crediting of righteousness happens before Abraham is circumcised (Genesis 17) or before the Law is given, establishing faith as the timeless way of being right with God.

questions.question: What Scripture passages teach the doctrine of original sin?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 5:12, Rom 5:18-19, Ps 51:5, Gen 3:6-7
questions.response:
The doctrine of original sin is primarily derived from a combination of biblical narratives, wisdom literature, and apostolic teachings. While the term "original sin" itself is not in the Bible, the concept is understood as the fallen state of human nature inherited from Adam, which results in spiritual death and a propensity toward sin.

Here are the key Scripture passages that teach this doctrine, grouped by their role in the theological framework.

### 1. The Foundational Narrative (The Fall)

This passage provides the historical and theological basis for the entrance of sin and death into the human race.

- **Genesis 3:1-19** : This is the account of the disobedience of Adam and Eve. Key elements include the temptation, the act of eating the forbidden fruit, and the resulting curses. Crucially, the curses (pain in childbearing, toil in work, and physical death) are not just individual punishments but affect the entire created order and all subsequent humanity. The expulsion from the Garden and the Tree of Life (3:22-24) signifies the new state of separation from God.

### 2. The Transmission of Sin and Death Through Adam

These New Testament passages explicitly connect Adam's single transgression to the sinful and mortal condition of all humanity.

- **Romans 5:12-19** : This is the most critical and systematic text on original sin.
    - **Verse 12:** "Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned..."
    - Paul argues that sin and death are universal powers that entered the world through Adam. The phrase "because all sinned" is often interpreted to mean that all humanity participated in Adam's sin seminally or representatively, and thus inherit a sinful nature and its consequence, which is death. The entire passage contrasts Adam, whose disobedience brought condemnation and death to all, with Christ, whose obedience brings justification and life.

- **1 Corinthians 15:21-22** : "For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive."
    - This passage solidifies the federal headship of Adam. His action had universal consequences for all who are "in him," just as Christ's actions have universal consequences for all who are "in Him." The death spoken of here is both physical and spiritual.

### 3. The Inherent Sinfulness of Human Nature

These texts describe the inward condition of humanity as universally sinful from the start of life, not merely as a result of imitating bad examples.

- **Psalm 51:5** : "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me."
    - David is not saying his conception was an act of sin, but that he was a sinner from the very moment of his existence. His sinful nature predates any personal, willful acts of sin. This points to an inherited moral corruption.

- **Ephesians 2:1-3** : "And you were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked... among whom we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the body and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind."
    - Paul states that the unregenerate state is one of spiritual death ("dead in trespasses"). Crucially, he says this is a condition we have "by nature." This fallen nature is not something we acquire through imitation but is intrinsic to our humanity post-Fall, making us objects of God's righteous wrath.

### 4. The Universal Reign of Sin

These passages emphasize that sin is not an occasional misstep but a universal, enslaving power that defines the human condition.

- **Genesis 6:5** : "The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually."
    - This pre-flood assessment shows the totality of human corruption. It's not just actions but the very "intentions of the thoughts" that are corrupted, pointing to a deeply rooted, inherent condition.

- **Romans 3:10-12, 23** : "None is righteous, no, not one; no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one... for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God."
    - This universal indictment confirms that the condition described in Genesis 6:5 and Psalm 51:5 is the reality for every human being without exception.

In summary, the doctrine of original sin is built on the narrative of the Fall in **Genesis 3**, with its consequences for human nature described in **Psalm 51:5** and **Ephesians 2:1-3**, and its transmission through Adam definitively explained in **Romans 5:12-19** and **1 Corinthians 15:21-22**.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the doctrine of the Trinity?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, 2 Cor 13:14, John 1:1, Gen 1:26
questions.response:
The word "Trinity" is not found in the Bible, but the doctrine is a systematic summary of what the entire Bible teaches about the nature of God. It is derived from three clear, simultaneous truths that Scripture presents:

1.  There is only one God.
2.  The Father, the Son (Jesus), and the Holy Spirit are each distinct persons.
3.  The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each fully and equally God.

Here is where the Bible teaches these foundational truths, organized by category.

---

### 1. The Bible Teaches There is Only One God (Monotheism)

This is the non-negotiable foundation inherited from the Old Testament.

- **Deuteronomy 6:4:** "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one."
- **Isaiah 44:6:** "Thus says the Lord, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, the Lord of hosts: 'I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god.'"
- **1 Corinthians 8:4:** "Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that 'an idol has no real existence,' and that 'there is no God but one.'"
- **James 2:19:** "You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder!"

---

### 2. The Bible Teaches the Three Persons are Distinct from One Another

The Father, Son, and Spirit are not simply three names or modes of the same person. They relate to one another and are distinguished from one another.

- **Distinction between Father and Son:** Jesus prays to the Father and speaks of the Father as another who sent him.
    - **John 17:1-3:** "When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, 'Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you...'"
    - **John 8:17-18:** "In your Law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me."
- **Distinction of the Spirit from the Father and Son:** The Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son and acts as a personal agent.
    - **John 14:26:** "But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things..."
    - **John 15:26:** "But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me."
- **All Three Distinct at Once:** The most famous example is at Jesus' baptism.
    - **Matthew 3:16-17:** "And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him; and behold, a voice from heaven said, 'This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.'" (The Son is in the water, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven).

---

### 3. The Bible Teaches Each Person is Fully God

The doctrine of the Trinity is not that God is one person who is one-third Father, one-third Son, and one-third Spirit. It is that each distinct person is fully and completely the one God.

#### The Father is God
This is universally accepted and clearly taught.
- **John 6:27:** "Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal."
- **1 Peter 1:2:** "...according to the foreknowledge of God the Father..."

#### The Son (Jesus Christ) is God
- **He is explicitly called God:**
    - **John 1:1, 14:** "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us..."
    - **John 20:28:** Thomas said to Jesus, "My Lord and my God!"
    - **Titus 2:13:** "...waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ."
    - **Hebrews 1:8:** "But of the Son he says, 'Your throne, O God, is forever and ever...'"
- **He possesses divine attributes and performs divine works:**
    - **Creator of all things:** **John 1:3** ("All things were made through him..."), **Colossians 1:16** ("For by him all things were created...")
    - **Eternal:** **Micah 5:2** ("...whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days."), **John 8:58** ("Before Abraham was, I am.")
    - **Receives worship due only to God:** **Hebrews 1:6** ("Let all God's angels worship him."), **Philippians 2:10-11** ("...at the name of Jesus every knee should bow...")
    - **Forgives sins:** **Mark 2:5-7** (The scribes rightly ask, "Who can forgive sins but God alone?")

#### The Holy Spirit is God
- **He is explicitly called God:**
    - **Acts 5:3-4:** Peter says to Ananias, "Why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit... You have not lied to man but to God." Lying to the Holy Spirit is equated with lying to God.
- **He possesses divine attributes and performs divine works:**
    - **Eternal:** **Hebrews 9:14** ("...who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God.")
    - **Omnipresent:** **Psalm 139:7-8** ("Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence?")
    - **Creator:** **Genesis 1:2** ("And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters."), **Job 33:4** ("The Spirit of God has made me...")
    - **He is a person, not an impersonal force:** He can be grieved (**Ephesians 4:30**), he speaks (**Acts 13:2**), he teaches (**John 14:26**), and he has a will (**1 Corinthians 12:11**).

---

### 4. Passages that Weave the Three Together

Some texts bring the three persons together in a formula that implies their equality and unity, which became the basis for the Trinitarian baptismal formula and doxologies.

- **Matthew 28:19 (The Great Commission):** "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in **the name** (singular, one God) of the **Father** and of the **Son** and of the **Holy Spirit**."
- **2 Corinthians 13:14 (The Apostolic Benediction):** "The grace of the **Lord Jesus Christ** and the love of **God** [the Father] and the fellowship of the **Holy Spirit** be with you all."
- **1 Peter 1:2:** "...according to the foreknowledge of **God the Father**, in the sanctification of the **Spirit**, for obedience to **Jesus Christ** and for sprinkling with his blood..."

In summary, the Bible does not offer a single "Trinity proof-text." Instead, the doctrine is a necessary theological conclusion drawn from the totality of Scripture, which consistently reveals the one true God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

questions.question: What passages affirm the full deity of Jesus Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: John 1:1, John 1:14, Col 2:9, Heb 1:3, Phil 2:6
questions.response:
Here are key New Testament passages that explicitly or implicitly affirm the full deity of Jesus Christ, demonstrating that He is identified as God, possesses divine attributes, and performs divine works.

### Direct Statements of Identity

**John 1:1-3, 14**
> "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was with God in the beginning. Through him all things were made... The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us."

This is one of the most direct statements. The Word (Jesus) is explicitly called "God" and is identified as the eternal Creator.

**John 20:28**
> "Thomas said to him, 'My Lord and my God!'"

Thomas addresses Jesus directly with the Greek words *ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou* (the Lord of me and the God of me). Jesus accepts this worship without correction.

**Titus 2:13**
> "...while we wait for the blessed hope—the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ."

In the Greek grammatical construction (Granville Sharp's rule), "God" and "Savior" both refer to the same person, Jesus Christ.

**Hebrews 1:8**
> "But about the Son he says, 'Your throne, O God, will last for ever and ever; a scepter of justice will be the scepter of your kingdom.'"

Here, God the Father addresses the Son as "O God," a direct quotation from Psalm 45:6 applied to Jesus.

**2 Peter 1:1**
> "...To those who through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours."

Similar to Titus 2:13, the grammar identifies Jesus Christ as "our God and Savior."

**Romans 9:5**
> "...the Messiah, who is God over all, forever praised! Amen."

Paul refers to Christ as "God over all," a clear ascription of deity.

**Colossians 2:9**
> "For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity lives in bodily form."

This passage states that the complete, undiminished nature of God dwells permanently in the incarnate Christ.

### Jesus' Own Claims

**John 8:58**
> "'Very truly I tell you,' Jesus answered, 'before Abraham was born, I am!'"

Jesus uses the divine name "I AM" (*ego eimi*), echoing God's self-identification in Exodus 3:14. The reaction of the Jews—picking up stones to kill Him for blasphemy—shows they understood this as a claim to deity.

**John 10:30-33**
> "I and the Father are one... The Jews answered him, 'We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because you, a mere man, claim to be God.'"

Jesus claims essential unity with the Father, and His audience clearly interprets this as a claim to be God. Jesus does not deny their interpretation.

**Mark 14:61-64**
> "Again the high priest asked him, 'Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?' 'I am,' said Jesus. 'And you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Mighty One and coming on the clouds of heaven.' The high priest tore his clothes. 'Why do we need any more witnesses?' he asked. 'You have heard the blasphemy.'"

Jesus combines the divine title "I AM" with the prophecy of Daniel 7:13-14, where the Son of Man receives eternal worship and dominion. The high priest recognizes this as a claim to divinity.

### Divine Attributes and Works

**John 5:21-23**
> "For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so the Son gives life to whom he is pleased to give it. Moreover, the Father judges no one, but has entrusted all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father."

Jesus claims the divine prerogatives of giving life and executing final judgment, and demands honor equal to that given to the Father.

**Matthew 28:18-19**
> "Then Jesus came to them and said, 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.'"

Jesus claims universal, omnipotent authority and places Himself on an equal level with the Father and the Spirit in the singular "name" of the triune God.

**Philippians 2:5-11**
> "Who, being in very nature God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage... that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow... and every tongue acknowledge that Jesus Christ is Lord."

This passage states that Jesus existed in the "form of God" prior to the incarnation and will receive universal worship, which is due to God alone (Isaiah 45:23).

**Revelation 1:17-18; 22:13**
> "I am the First and the Last. I am the Living One; I was dead, and now look, I am alive for ever and ever!"
> "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End."

Jesus applies to Himself the title "the First and the Last," which is used exclusively by Yahweh in Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12.

**Colossians 1:16-17**
> "For in him all things were created: things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible... all things have been created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together."

Jesus is identified as the agent, sustainer, and goal of all creation—a role ascribed only to God.

**Hebrews 1:3**
> "The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of his being, sustaining all things by his powerful word."

Jesus is the perfect, exact imprint of God's essential nature and sustains the universe, a divine function.

### Worship Given to Jesus

Worship (*proskyneō*) is reserved for God alone (Matthew 4:10), yet Jesus receives worship repeatedly without rebuke:
- The disciples worship Him after He walks on water (Matthew 14:33).
- A healed blind man worships Him (John 9:38).
- The women at the tomb worship the resurrected Christ (Matthew 28:9).
- All of heaven worships the Lamb (Revelation 5:12-14).

questions.question: Which Bible passages teach the bodily resurrection of Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Cor 15:3-8, Matt 28:5-6, Luke 24:39, John 20:27
questions.response:
Here are several key Bible passages that Christians point to as teaching the bodily, physical resurrection of Jesus Christ:

### 1. The Empty Tomb Narratives
These passages emphasize that the physical body of Jesus was no longer in the tomb.

- **Matthew 28:1–10**: The angel tells the women, "He is not here; he has risen, just as he said. Come and see the place where he lay." Later, the women clasp his feet and worship him.
- **Mark 16:1–8**: A young man in a white robe tells the women, "You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen! He is not here. See the place where they laid him."
- **Luke 24:1–12**: Peter runs to the tomb, stoops down, and sees the strips of linen lying by themselves, indicating the body was gone, not merely a spirit.
- **John 20:1–9**: The "other disciple" (John) sees the linen wrappings and the face cloth folded up by itself, and he "saw and believed."

### 2. Post-Resurrection Appearances Emphasizing Physicality
Jesus goes out of his way to demonstrate he is not a ghost or a vision, but has flesh and bones.

- **Luke 24:36–43**: Jesus appears to the terrified disciples and says, "Look at my hands and my feet. It is I myself! Touch me and see; a ghost does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have." To further prove his physical nature, he asks for something to eat and eats a piece of broiled fish in their presence.
- **John 20:24–28**: Thomas, who doubted, is invited by Jesus to put his finger into the nail marks and his hand into the wound in his side. Thomas responds, "My Lord and my God!"
- **John 21:1–14**: Jesus appears on the shore of the Sea of Galilee and cooks a breakfast of fish and bread for the disciples, which they eat together.

### 3. The Theological Argument for a Physical Body
The Apostle Paul argues that a physical resurrection is essential to the Christian faith and defines the nature of the resurrected body.

- **1 Corinthians 15:3–8**: Paul recites the early creed that Christ "was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures" and appeared to Peter, the Twelve, more than 500 brothers at once, James, all the apostles, and lastly to Paul himself.
- **1 Corinthians 15:12–23**: Paul directly links Christ's bodily resurrection to the future resurrection of believers. He argues, "If there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile."
- **1 Corinthians 15:35–44**: Paul describes the resurrection body as a "spiritual body" (not meaning non-physical, but a body transformed and empowered by the Spirit), contrasting the perishable "natural body" with the imperishable "spiritual body," using Christ as the prototype.

### 4. The Witness of the Apostles
The early preaching in Acts consistently focuses on the physical resurrection as a fulfillment of prophecy and a historical event.

- **Acts 2:24–32**: Peter, at Pentecost, argues that David spoke of the resurrection of the Messiah, saying, "he was not abandoned to the realm of the dead, nor did his body see decay." Peter emphasizes, "God has raised this Jesus to life, and we are all witnesses of it."
- **Acts 10:40–41**: Peter tells Cornelius that God raised Jesus on the third day and "caused him to be seen... by us who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead."

These passages collectively form the basis for the Christian doctrine that Jesus's resurrection was not merely a spiritual or metaphorical event, but a literal, physical raising of his crucified body to a new, glorified, and immortal state.

questions.question: What Scripture supports the doctrine of substitutionary atonement?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Isa 53:5-6, 2 Cor 5:21, 1 Pet 2:24, Rom 3:25
questions.response:
The doctrine of substitutionary atonement—that Christ died as a substitute for sinners, bearing their punishment to satisfy divine justice—is supported by a rich tapestry of Scripture across both the Old and New Testaments. Here are the key passages, organized by theme:

### 1. The Old Testament Foundation: The Sacrificial System

The entire Levitical system, particularly the Day of Atonement, prefigures substitution. The sinner identified with the sacrifice by laying hands on it, symbolically transferring guilt before the animal was slain.

- **Leviticus 16:21-22** – The scapegoat ritual is a vivid picture of substitution: "And Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel, and all their transgressions, all their sins. And he shall put them on the head of the goat... The goat shall bear all their iniquities on itself to a remote area."
- **Leviticus 17:11** – Establishes the principle of life-for-life substitution: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life."

### 2. The Great Prophetic Portrait: Isaiah 53

This chapter is the most explicit and detailed Old Testament prophecy of substitutionary atonement, using unmistakable language of transfer and bearing.

- **Isaiah 53:4-6** – "Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows... he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities... the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all."
- **Isaiah 53:8** – "...stricken for the transgression of my people."
- **Isaiah 53:10-12** – "His soul makes an offering for guilt... he shall bear their iniquities... he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors."

### 3. The Words of Christ Himself

Jesus explicitly interpreted his own death as a substitutionary ransom and a sacrifice for others.

- **Mark 10:45** – "For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many." The word "for" (Greek *anti*) means "in place of."
- **Matthew 26:28** – At the Last Supper, Jesus says, "For this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins." This directly connects his death to the sacrificial system.

### 4. The Apostolic Teaching in the Epistles

The apostles make the doctrine explicit, using precise theological language.

- **2 Corinthians 5:21** – The "Great Exchange" verse: "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God." Christ was treated as a sinner in our place.
- **Galatians 3:13** – "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, 'Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree.'" He absorbed the law's curse as our substitute.
- **1 Peter 2:24** – "He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness." The language of "bearing" sin echoes Isaiah 53.
- **1 Peter 3:18** – "For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God." The preposition "for" (Greek *hyper*) clearly indicates substitution.
- **Romans 3:25** – God put Christ forward "as a propitiation by his blood." The word *hilastērion* (propitiation) means a sacrifice that turns away and absorbs God's righteous wrath against sin.
- **Hebrews 9:28** – "So Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many..." Again, the direct language of bearing sin.

### 5. The Typology of the Passover Lamb

The New Testament identifies Christ with the Passover lamb, whose blood shielded Israel from judgment.

- **1 Corinthians 5:7** – "For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed." The lamb died in place of the firstborn.
- **John 1:29** – John the Baptist declares, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!" The lamb imagery is inherently substitutionary.

Together, these passages form a unified biblical witness: humanity's sin deserves divine judgment, but Christ voluntarily took that penalty upon himself, satisfying justice and securing forgiveness for all who trust in him.

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach the imputation of Christ's righteousness?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 2 Cor 5:21, Rom 4:3-6, Phil 3:9, Rom 5:19
questions.response:
The doctrine of the imputation of Christ's righteousness is primarily derived from several key passages in the New Testament, particularly in the writings of the Apostle Paul. Here are the central texts and the reasoning behind this teaching:

### 1. 2 Corinthians 5:21
**"For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God."**
This verse is often considered the clearest statement of the double imputation: our sin is imputed (credited) to Christ on the cross, and His righteousness is imputed to us. The exchange is forensic—a legal declaration—not an infusion of moral quality.

### 2. Romans 4:3–8 (cf. Genesis 15:6)
**"Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness."**
Paul argues that righteousness was "counted" (Greek: *logizomai*, meaning to reckon or credit) to Abraham through faith, not works. He then extends this to all believers, emphasizing that God "justifies the ungodly" by crediting righteousness apart from works. David is cited as another example of the person to whom God credits righteousness apart from works (Psalm 32:1–2).

### 3. Romans 5:12–19 (especially vv. 18–19)
**"Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous."**
Paul draws a parallel between Adam and Christ. Adam’s sin was imputed to his descendants, resulting in condemnation. In the same way, Christ’s righteous act (His obedient life and death) is imputed to those who are in Him, resulting in justification. This is a covenantal, representative imputation.

### 4. Philippians 3:8–9
**"…not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith."**
Paul contrasts a righteousness based on his own law-keeping with a righteousness that is "from God" and received by faith. This is an alien righteousness, not an inherent one, which is credited to the believer.

### 5. Romans 3:21–26
**"But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law… the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe."**
Here, "the righteousness of God" is understood not merely as God’s own attribute, but as a righteous status He provides and credits to the believer through faith in Christ. This is linked to Christ’s propitiatory sacrifice, showing that the basis of imputation is Christ’s atoning work.

### 6. 1 Corinthians 1:30
**"And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption."**
Christ Himself is described as our righteousness. Union with Him means that what He is and has done is counted as ours.

### Theological Summary
The imputation of Christ’s righteousness rests on the biblical concepts of:
- **Representation:** Christ acts as the federal head of a new humanity (Romans 5; 1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45–49).
- **Forensic declaration:** Justification is a legal verdict, not a process of moral transformation (Romans 3:24, 28; 8:33–34).
- **Faith as instrument:** Righteousness is received by faith alone, not by works (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16).
- **The great exchange:** Our sin is laid on Christ, and His righteousness is credited to us (2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13–14).

These passages, taken together, form the biblical foundation for the teaching that believers are justified by the imputed righteousness of Christ, received through faith alone.

questions.question: What passages describe the process of sanctification?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Thess 4:3, Phil 2:12-13, 2 Cor 3:18, Heb 12:14
questions.response:
Sanctification is a central theme in Christian theology, referring to the process by which a believer is set apart for God and progressively transformed into the likeness of Christ. The Bible describes this process as a work of God involving the believer's active participation. Here are key passages that describe the process of sanctification, grouped by their emphasis.

---

### 1. The Foundation and Definition of Sanctification

These passages establish that sanctification is God's will and a definitive act of being set apart, as well as a progressive work.

- **1 Corinthians 6:11** – A definitive, positional sanctification that happens at salvation.
  > "And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God."

- **Hebrews 10:10, 14** – Sanctification as a once-for-all act through Christ's sacrifice, with ongoing results.
  > "And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all... For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified."

- **1 Thessalonians 4:3** – Sanctification as God's explicit will for believers, particularly in moral purity.
  > "For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality."

---

### 2. The Agent and Means of Sanctification

These passages highlight who does the sanctifying and the instruments used.

- **God the Father:**
  - **1 Thessalonians 5:23** – God is the one who sanctifies the whole person.
    > "Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ."

- **Jesus Christ:**
  - **Hebrews 2:11** – Jesus is the one who sanctifies.
    > "For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all have one source. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers."
  - **Ephesians 5:25-27** – Christ sanctifies the church through His word.
    > "...Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word."

- **The Holy Spirit:**
  - **2 Thessalonians 2:13** – Sanctification is a work of the Spirit.
    > "...God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth."
  - **Romans 15:16** – The Holy Spirit sanctifies believers.
    > "...to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit."

- **The Word of God (Truth):**
  - **John 17:17** – Jesus prays for believers' sanctification through God's truth.
    > "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth."

---

### 3. The Progressive and Cooperative Nature of Sanctification

These passages show that sanctification is a process requiring the believer's active pursuit, empowered by God.

- **Romans 6:19, 22** – A call to present oneself as a slave to righteousness, leading to sanctification.
  > "...now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification... But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life."

- **2 Corinthians 7:1** – A call to cleanse oneself from defilement, perfecting holiness.
  > "Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God."

- **Philippians 2:12-13** – The divine-human cooperation: believers work out their salvation because God is at work in them.
  > "...work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure."

- **Hebrews 12:14** – A command to actively pursue holiness.
  > "Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord."

- **2 Peter 1:5-8** – A call to diligently add virtues to faith, describing a progressive growth in godly character.
  > "For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love. For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ."

---

### 4. The Goal and Pattern of Sanctification

These passages describe the ultimate aim of sanctification: conformity to the image of Christ.

- **Romans 8:29** – The ultimate purpose is to be conformed to Christ's image.
  > "For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers."

- **2 Corinthians 3:18** – A continuous transformation into Christ's likeness by the Spirit.
  > "And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit."

- **Colossians 3:9-10** – The new self is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its Creator.
  > "...seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator."

- **1 John 3:2-3** – The hope of being like Christ at His appearing motivates present purification.
  > "Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure."

These passages together paint a comprehensive picture: sanctification is a definitive act of God at salvation, a progressive work of the Triune God using His Word and Spirit, a cooperative process where believers actively pursue holiness, and a journey with the ultimate goal of being conformed to the image of Jesus Christ.

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about the means of grace?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Rom 10:17, Acts 2:42, 1 Cor 11:23-26, Matt 28:19
questions.response:
The concept of the “means of grace” refers to the instruments or channels through which God, by His Spirit, delivers the forgiveness of sins, life, and salvation won by Christ’s death and resurrection. While the precise phrase “means of grace” is an extra-biblical theological term, the reality it describes is taught throughout Scripture.

The foundational means are the Word and the Sacraments (Baptism and the Lord’s Supper). In some traditions, the Office of the Keys (confession and absolution) and prayer are also understood in this context. Here is where Scripture teaches these truths:

### 1. The Word of God
Scripture teaches that the Word of God is not merely informational but life-giving and effective. It is the primary means by which the Holy Spirit creates and sustains faith.

- **Isaiah 55:10-11:** “For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth, making it bring forth and sprout… so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it.”
- **Romans 10:17:** “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.”
- **2 Timothy 3:15:** “And how from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.”
- **1 Peter 1:23:** “Since you have been born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God.”

### 2. Holy Baptism
Scripture teaches that Baptism is a washing of regeneration in which God applies the merits of Christ to an individual.

- **Matthew 28:19:** “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” (Baptism is the divinely commanded act of making disciples, linking it to salvation).
- **Acts 2:38-39:** “And Peter said to them, ‘Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and for your children…’” (Baptism is connected directly to the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Spirit).
- **Romans 6:3-4:** “Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.” (Baptism unites the believer with Christ’s saving death and resurrection).
- **Titus 3:5:** “He saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit.” (This “washing” is a clear reference to Baptism as the means of regeneration).

### 3. The Lord’s Supper (Holy Communion)
Scripture teaches that in this sacrament, Christ’s true body and blood are given with the bread and wine for the forgiveness of sins.

- **Matthew 26:26-28:** “Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and after blessing it, broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said, ‘Take, eat; this is my body.’ And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, ‘Drink of it, all of you, for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.’” (Christ directly links the elements to His body and blood and their purpose to forgiveness).
- **1 Corinthians 10:16:** “The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?” (The word “participation” or “communion” (koinonia) indicates a real sharing in Christ’s body and blood).
- **1 Corinthians 11:28-29:** “Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.” (This severe warning only makes sense if Christ’s body is truly present, making an unworthy reception a sin against the body and blood of the Lord).

### 4. The Office of the Keys (Confession and Absolution)
Many traditions see the public and private proclamation of absolution as a specific application of the Word, returning the believer to the grace of their Baptism.

- **Matthew 16:19:** “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.”
- **John 20:22-23:** “And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld.’” (Christ gives His authority to forgive sins to His church, to be exercised by His called ministers).

### Summary
Scripture presents these instruments not as mere rituals or symbols, but as the actual delivery vehicles of the salvation Christ accomplished. They are the means by which Christ, through the Holy Spirit, comes to His people to give, seal, and strengthen faith. As the Book of Acts records, the early church devoted themselves to these very means: “And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42).

questions.question: What Bible passages support covenant theology?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Gen 17:7, Jer 31:31-34, Heb 8:6-13, Gal 3:29
questions.response:
Covenant theology is a framework for understanding the Bible's story, emphasizing that God relates to humanity through a series of covenants. Here are key Bible passages that support its major tenets, organized by the covenants they represent.

### 1. The Covenant of Redemption (Intra-Trinitarian)
This covenant, made in eternity past, is an agreement between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to accomplish salvation. While not explicitly named, it is deduced from passages showing the Father's plan and the Son's mission.

- **Ephesians 1:3-14:** The Father chooses, the Son redeems through His blood, and the Spirit seals. The entire plan of salvation is rooted in God's eternal purpose.
- **John 17:1-26:** Jesus, in His high priestly prayer, speaks of the work the Father gave Him to do, the people the Father gave Him, and the glory He shared with the Father before the world existed.
- **Hebrews 13:20:** "Now may the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant..." This points to a covenant that transcends time.

### 2. The Covenant of Works (with Adam)
This covenant was made with Adam as the representative head of all humanity, promising life for obedience and threatening death for disobedience.

- **Genesis 2:16-17:** The foundational command and sanction. "And the Lord God commanded the man, saying, 'You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die.'"
- **Hosea 6:7:** "But like Adam they transgressed the covenant; there they dealt faithlessly with me." This directly calls Adam's arrangement a "covenant."
- **Romans 5:12-21:** Paul's parallel between Adam and Christ. Adam's one trespass led to condemnation for all, establishing him as a federal head in a works-based arrangement, which Christ fulfills and remedies.

### 3. The Covenant of Grace
After the fall, God established the Covenant of Grace, promising salvation through faith in a Redeemer. This one covenant is progressively revealed and administered through various biblical covenants.

#### The Noahic Covenant (Common Grace and Preservation)
This covenant guarantees the stability of the created order, providing the stage for the unfolding of redemption.

- **Genesis 6:18:** "But I will establish my covenant with you..." The first explicit use of "covenant" (*berith*).
- **Genesis 9:8-17:** The covenant is made with Noah, his descendants, and every living creature, with the rainbow as its sign, promising never to destroy the earth by flood again.

#### The Abrahamic Covenant (Promise and Family)
This covenant is central, promising Abraham a seed (offspring), land, and that through him all nations would be blessed. It reveals the gracious, promissory nature of salvation.

- **Genesis 12:1-3:** The initial promise of blessing, a great name, and a channel of blessing to all families of the earth.
- **Genesis 15:1-21:** The formal covenant ratification. God alone passes through the animal pieces, signifying a unilateral, unconditional promise. Verse 6 is key: "And he believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness."
- **Genesis 17:1-14:** The covenant is reaffirmed, names are changed, and circumcision is given as the sign and seal of the covenant.
- **Galatians 3:6-9, 16-18, 29:** Paul interprets the Abrahamic covenant as the gospel announced beforehand, centered on Christ (the singular "seed"), and received by faith, not works of the law. Believers in Christ are Abraham's spiritual offspring.

#### The Mosaic Covenant (Law and Condemnation)
This covenant is a critical point of interpretation. Covenant theology sees it as an administration of the Covenant of Grace, where the moral law serves to drive people to Christ, while its ceremonial aspects foreshadow Him.

- **Exodus 19:5-6:** The conditional framework: "Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession..."
- **Exodus 24:1-8:** The covenant is ratified with blood, and the people pledge obedience. The book of the covenant is read.
- **Deuteronomy 4:13:** "And he declared to you his covenant, which he commanded you to perform, that is, the Ten Commandments..."
- **Galatians 3:19-24:** Paul explains the Mosaic law was "added because of transgressions" and was a "guardian" or "tutor" to lead us to Christ so that we might be justified by faith. It was temporary and pedagogical.

#### The Davidic Covenant (Kingdom and King)
This covenant promises David an eternal dynasty, throne, and kingdom, ultimately fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the Son of David.

- **2 Samuel 7:12-16:** God promises to establish the throne of David's offspring forever. "I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son."
- **Psalm 89:3-4, 34-37:** A poetic celebration of the covenant's permanence, even in the face of unfaithfulness.
- **Isaiah 55:3:** "Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live; and I will make with you an everlasting covenant, my steadfast, sure love for David."
- **Luke 1:31-33:** The angel Gabriel tells Mary that Jesus will be given "the throne of his father David... and of his kingdom there will be no end."

#### The New Covenant (Fulfillment and Consummation)
This is the final, complete, and efficacious administration of the Covenant of Grace, in which Christ fulfills all previous covenants.

- **Jeremiah 31:31-34:** The definitive prophecy. It promises a new covenant unlike the Mosaic one, characterized by the law written on hearts, a direct knowledge of God, and the full forgiveness of sins. This passage is quoted extensively in Hebrews 8:8-12 and 10:16-17.
- **Ezekiel 36:26-27:** The promise of a new heart and the indwelling Spirit, enabling obedience.
- **Luke 22:20:** At the Last Supper, Jesus declares, "This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood."
- **Hebrews 7:22, 8:6, 9:15, 12:24:** Jesus is the "guarantor of a better covenant," the "mediator of a new covenant," and His blood is "the blood of the eternal covenant." The entire book of Hebrews is an extended treatise on the superiority and finality of the New Covenant in Christ.

These passages collectively demonstrate the unified structure of covenant theology: a God who condescends to relate to His creation through binding agreements, all of which find their ultimate "Yes" and "Amen" in Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).

questions.question: Where does the Bible teach about the Lord's Supper?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Cor 11:23-26, Matt 26:26-28, Luke 22:19-20
questions.response:
The Bible teaches about the Lord's Supper in several key passages, primarily in the New Testament. Here are the main places where it is instituted, explained, and practiced:

### 1. The Institution by Jesus (The Gospels)
The actual event of Jesus establishing the Lord's Supper during the Last Supper is recorded in the Synoptic Gospels:

- **Matthew 26:26-29** – "While they were eating, Jesus took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to his disciples, saying, 'Take and eat; this is my body.' Then he took a cup, and when he had given thanks, he gave it to them, saying, 'Drink from it, all of you. This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins...'"
- **Mark 14:22-25** – A parallel account to Matthew's, using very similar language.
- **Luke 22:14-20** – Luke's account includes the specific command, "Do this in remembrance of me."

### 2. The Teaching and Practice in the Early Church (1 Corinthians)
The Apostle Paul provides the most detailed theological teaching on the Lord's Supper, correcting abuses and explaining its meaning. This is the most extensive passage on the subject:

- **1 Corinthians 11:23-34** – Paul recounts the tradition he received from the Lord, directly quoting Jesus's words of institution. He then teaches on the importance of self-examination before partaking, the meaning of proclaiming the Lord's death, and the serious nature of participating in an unworthy manner. He writes, "For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes" (v. 26).

### 3. Its Connection to Christian Unity (1 Corinthians)
Earlier in the same letter, Paul connects the Lord's Supper (also called "the Lord's table") to the unity of the church as the body of Christ:

- **1 Corinthians 10:16-17, 21** – "Is not the cup of thanksgiving for which we give thanks a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one loaf, we, who are many, are one body, for we all share the one loaf." He also contrasts the "cup of the Lord" and the "Lord's table" with pagan sacrifices.

### 4. Possible Early References in Acts
The practice of the very first church in Jerusalem is described in Acts, which many understand to include the Lord's Supper as part of their fellowship:

- **Acts 2:42, 46** – "They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer." ... "They broke bread in their homes and ate together with glad and sincere hearts." While "breaking of bread" can refer to a common meal, in this context it is widely seen as including the Lord's Supper.
- **Acts 20:7, 11** – In Troas, the believers gathered "on the first day of the week... to break bread," and Paul spoke to them. This indicates the practice was a regular part of their worship.

In summary, the **Gospels** record the historical institution, while **1 Corinthians** provides the doctrinal explanation and practical instructions for the church. **Acts** shows the early church faithfully observing it.

questions.question: What passages address the doctrine of baptism?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Matt 28:19, Acts 2:38-39, Rom 6:3-4, Col 2:11-12
questions.response:
The doctrine of baptism is addressed in numerous passages throughout the New Testament. These passages can be grouped by their theological emphasis: the command to be baptized, its meaning as identification with Christ's death and resurrection, its connection to repentance and forgiveness, and its role in salvation and the church.

Here is a categorized list of key passages:

### 1. The Command and Institution of Baptism
These passages establish baptism as an ordinance commanded by Christ for all who become his disciples.

- **Matthew 28:18-20 (The Great Commission):** "Then Jesus came to them and said, 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, **baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit**, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you.'"
- **Mark 16:15-16:** "He said to them, 'Go into all the world and preach the gospel to all creation. **Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved**, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.'"

### 2. The Meaning of Baptism: Union with Christ
These passages explain the deep spiritual symbolism of baptism, portraying it as a participation in the death, burial, and resurrection of Jesus.

- **Romans 6:3-5 (The central text on the meaning of baptism):** "Or don’t you know that all of us who were **baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death**? We were therefore **buried with him through baptism into death** in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may live a new life. For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we will certainly also be united with him in a resurrection like his."
- **Colossians 2:11-12:** "In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not performed by human hands. Your whole self, ruled by the flesh, was put off when you were circumcised by Christ, **having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him** through your faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead."
- **Galatians 3:26-27:** "So in Christ Jesus you are all children of God through faith, for all of you who were **baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ**."

### 3. Baptism, Repentance, and Forgiveness of Sins
These passages closely link baptism with the inward reality of repentance and the promise of forgiveness.

- **Acts 2:38 (Peter's response at Pentecost):** "Peter replied, '**Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins**. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.'"
- **Acts 22:16 (Ananias's words to Paul):** "And now what are you waiting for? Get up, **be baptized and wash your sins away, calling on his name**."
- **1 Peter 3:21 (Baptism as an appeal to God):** "...and this water symbolizes baptism that now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the body but **the pledge of a clear conscience toward God**. It saves you by the resurrection of Jesus Christ."

### 4. Baptism and the Gift of the Holy Spirit
Baptism is consistently associated with the reception of the Holy Spirit.

- **Acts 2:38:** (See above) "...Repent and be baptized... and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit."
- **Acts 19:1-6:** Paul finds disciples in Ephesus who had only received John's baptism. After being "baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus," Paul laid hands on them, and "the Holy Spirit came on them."
- **Titus 3:5:** "He saved us, not because of righteous things we had done, but because of his mercy. He saved us through the **washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit**."

### 5. The "One Baptism" and Unity of the Body
Baptism is a foundational element of Christian unity, as it is the common entry point for all believers into the one body of Christ.

- **Ephesians 4:4-6:** "There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to one hope when you were called; one Lord, one faith, **one baptism**; one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all."
- **1 Corinthians 12:13:** "For we were all **baptized by one Spirit so as to form one body**—whether Jews or Gentiles, slave or free—and we were all given the one Spirit to drink."

### 6. Examples of Baptism in the Early Church
The book of Acts provides a consistent pattern of immediate baptism upon faith in Christ.

- **Acts 2:41:** "Those who accepted his message were baptized, and about three thousand were added to their number that day."
- **Acts 8:12-13:** Philip preached in Samaria, and "when they believed Philip as he proclaimed the good news of the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Simon himself believed and was baptized."
- **Acts 8:36-38 (The Ethiopian Eunuch):** "As they traveled along the road, they came to some water and the eunuch said, 'Look, here is water. What can stand in the way of my being baptized?' ...Then both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water and Philip baptized him."
- **Acts 10:47-48 (Cornelius's Household):** After the Holy Spirit fell on the Gentiles, Peter said, "'Surely no one can stand in the way of their being baptized with water. They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have.' So he ordered that they be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ."
- **Acts 16:14-15 (Lydia):** "The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. When she and the members of her household were baptized..."
- **Acts 16:33 (The Philippian Jailer):** "At that hour of the night the jailer took them and washed their wounds; then immediately he and all his household were baptized."

questions.question: Where does Scripture teach about church government and eldership?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: 1 Tim 3:1-7, Titus 1:5-9, Acts 14:23, 1 Pet 5:1-4
questions.response:
The Bible’s teaching on church government and eldership is woven throughout the New Testament, established by the Old Testament, and rooted in the character of God. It's not found in a single chapter but in a cohesive set of passages that describe a pattern, qualifications, and a theology of leadership.

Here is a breakdown of where Scripture teaches on this topic, organized thematically.

---

### 1. The Old Testament Foundation

The New Testament concept of the elder (*presbyteros*) did not emerge in a vacuum. It was the established form of community leadership in Israel.

- **Exodus 18:13-27** – Jethro’s counsel to Moses establishes a critical principle: a plurality of capable, God-fearing men who share the burden of judging and leading the people. This shapes the NT idea of a leadership team, not a single ruler.
- **Numbers 11:16-17** – God commands Moses to gather 70 elders to bear the burden of the people with him. God takes some of the Spirit on Moses and puts it on them, signifying a shared spiritual authority.
- **The Synagogue Model** – While not a specific verse, the Jewish synagogue of the intertestamental period was universally governed by a council of elders. This was the immediate cultural and organizational pattern that the first Christians, who were Jewish, adapted for the church.

---

### 2. The Historical Pattern in Acts

The Book of Acts records the practice of the early church as the gospel spread. It shows a transition from Apostolic leadership to local elder leadership.

- **Acts 11:29-30** – The first mention of elders in the Jerusalem church, distinct from the apostles. Relief funds are sent "to the elders," indicating they were a recognized body responsible for practical administration.
- **Acts 14:23** – A foundational verse. On their first missionary journey, Paul and Barnabas, "appointed elders for them in every church," with prayer and fasting, entrusting them to the Lord. This establishes the pattern that a healthy church plant moves toward a plurality of elders.
- **Acts 15:2, 4, 6, 22, 23** – The Jerusalem Council. The critical doctrinal question of Gentile circumcision is addressed by "the apostles and elders," showing a shared governing body. The letter's salutation is "The apostles and elders, your brothers."
- **Acts 20:17, 28-31** – Paul summons the elders of the church in Ephesus. In his final charge, he reveals the core substance of their role by using three different Greek words:
    - "Elders" (*presbyteroi*, v. 17): The title indicating their mature, recognized status.
    - "Overseers" (*episkopoi*, v. 28): The role of guarding, leading, and shepherding.
    - "Shepherd" (*poimainō*, v. 28): The function of a pastor, which is to feed, protect, and care for the flock which God purchased with His own blood.

---

### 3. The Qualifications and Character (The "Who")

These are the most detailed passages, focusing not on what an elder *does* but on who an elder *is*. It's a profile of mature, masculine, gospel-changed character.

- **1 Timothy 3:1-7** – The qualifications for an "overseer" (*episkopos*).
    - He must be "above reproach," a "husband of one wife," sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, "able to teach."
    - He must not be a drunkard, violent, quarrelsome, or a lover of money.
    - He must manage his own household well, with dignified children, "for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?"
    - He must not be a recent convert.
    - He must be well thought of by outsiders.

- **Titus 1:5-9** – Paul left Titus in Crete to "appoint elders in every town." The qualifications mirror 1 Timothy but with a strong emphasis on doctrinal fidelity.
    - An elder must be "a steward of God," above reproach, with believing children not known for wildness.
    - Crucially, "He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it" (v. 9). This highlights the elder's role as a doctrinal guardian.

---

### 4. The Theology and Work of Eldership (The "What" and "How")

These passages teach the "why" and "how" of their spiritual work.

- **1 Peter 5:1-4** – Peter, an apostle who identifies himself as a "fellow elder," gives the core pastoral mandate.
    - The task: "Shepherd the flock of God that is among you."
    - The motive: Not under compulsion, not for shameful gain, but eagerly.
    - The manner: Not domineering over those in your charge, but "being examples to the flock."
    - The reward: When the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.
- **Ephesians 4:11-12** – The ascended Christ Himself gives "shepherds and teachers" (a combined role closely tied to elders) as a gift to the church. Their purpose is not to do all the ministry, but "to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ."
- **Hebrews 13:17** – This verse defines the relationship between the congregation and its leaders.
    - Leaders "keep watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account."
    - The congregation's response is to "Obey your leaders and submit to them," making their work a joy and not a burden. This authority is real but is bound to their God-given, accountable, watchman role.

---

### 5. The Plurality of Leadership

A consistent pattern, not just a suggestion, is that a biblically governed church is led by a plurality of elders.

- **Consistent Plurality in the New Testament:** Elders are always referred to in the plural in every church.
    - Jerusalem: "the apostles and the elders" (Acts 15:4).
    - Ephesus: "the elders *of the church*" (Acts 20:17).
    - Philippi: "the overseers and deacons" (Philippians 1:1).
    - Crete: "appoint elders in every town" (Titus 1:5).
    - The Diaspora: James instructs the sick person to call for "the elders of the church" (James 5:14).
- **Shared Leadership, Not a Singular Pastor:** This plurality reflects the shared life of the Triune God and provides accountability, shared wisdom, and a diversity of gifts. There is no example of a church being led by a single elder or a "senior pastor" who rules over other elders. The "first among equals" concept is a practical necessity for order, but it is subordinate to and accountable to the plurality.

---

### 6. The Office of Deacon: A Distinct and Closely Related Ministry

The biblical picture of church government is not complete without the deacon, whose role serves the elders' ministry of the Word and the physical needs of the body.

- **Acts 6:1-6** – While the title "deacon" isn't used, the seven men chosen to serve tables so the apostles can devote themselves "to prayer and to the ministry of the word" establishes the principle for the office. Elders shepherd the soul; deacons administer the physical needs, preserving the unity and witness of the church.
- **1 Timothy 3:8-13** – Immediately following the qualifications for overseers, Paul lists the qualifications for deacons. They must be dignified, not double-tongued, tested, and their wives must likewise be dignified. Their good service earns them a good standing and confidence in the faith.

Scripture, therefore, presents a government that is Christ-led, elder-overseen, deacon-served, and congregation-affirmed, all for the purpose of shepherding souls, guarding the gospel, and equipping the saints for the glory of the Chief Shepherd.

questions.question: What Bible passages teach about the second coming of Christ?
questions.reference_answer: Key passages: Acts 1:11, 1 Thess 4:16-17, Matt 24:30, Rev 1:7
questions.response:
The Bible contains many passages about the second coming of Christ, spanning both the Old and New Testaments. Here is a categorized overview of key teachings, with representative verses.

### 1. The Promise and Certainty of His Return
These passages establish that Jesus's return is a guaranteed future event, often given as a source of hope and comfort.

- **John 14:1-3** – Jesus himself promises to return for his disciples.
  > "And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also."

- **Acts 1:10-11** – Angels confirm that Jesus will return in the same way he ascended.
  > "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven."

- **Titus 2:13** – The return is called the "blessed hope."
  > "...waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ."

- **Hebrews 9:28** – Christ will appear a second time to save those who are waiting for him.
  > "...so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him."

### 2. The Manner of His Return
These passages describe *how* Jesus will return, emphasizing that it will be personal, visible, glorious, and unmistakable.

- **Matthew 24:27, 30** – It will be as visible as lightning and accompanied by great glory.
  > "For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man... Then will appear in heaven the sign of the Son of Man, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory."

- **Revelation 1:7** – Every eye will see him.
  > "Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him."

- **1 Thessalonians 4:16-17** – It will involve a loud command, the voice of an archangel, and the trumpet of God, with a resurrection of the dead and a catching up of living believers.
  > "For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord."

### 3. The Timing: Unknown and Sudden
The Bible consistently teaches that the exact time is unknowable, so believers must always be ready.

- **Matthew 24:36, 42-44** – No one knows the day or hour, so it will come unexpectedly.
  > "But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only... Therefore, stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming... the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect."

- **1 Thessalonians 5:1-3** – The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, suddenly and unexpectedly.
  > "For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. While people are saying, 'There is peace and security,' then sudden destruction will come upon them..."

- **2 Peter 3:10** – The day of the Lord will come like a thief.
  > "But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed."

### 4. The Purpose: Judgment and Salvation
The second coming serves a dual purpose: to bring final salvation to believers and judgment upon the ungodly.

- **Matthew 25:31-46** – The Son of Man will come in glory to separate people like a shepherd separates sheep from goats, based on their response to him.
  > "When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne. Before him will be gathered all the nations, and he will separate people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats."

- **2 Thessalonians 1:7-10** – Jesus will be revealed from heaven to grant relief to the afflicted and to inflict vengeance on those who do not obey the gospel.
  > "...when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus."

- **2 Timothy 4:1** – Christ Jesus is to judge the living and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom.
  > "I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom..."

### 5. Preparation: Watchfulness and Holy Living
The proper response to the promise of Christ's return is not speculation, but active, faithful, and holy living.
